title: Paksiw na tulingan
intro: Bullet tuna simmered slowly in vinegar, garlic and ginger until the dark, firm flesh soaks up the sour sauce. It is bold and tangy and keeps for days.

items.name: medium tulingan (bullet tuna)
items.note: about 1 kg in all, gutted and gills removed

steps.text: Rinse the fish well, especially along the dark bloodline, and cut each one in half crosswise.
Spread the garlic, ginger and onion in a heavy, non-reactive pot. Pack the fish on top and add the peppercorns, salt and chilies.
Pour in the vinegar and water and bring to a boil over medium heat, uncovered and without stirring.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the fish is firm all the way through.
Uncover, drizzle in the oil and simmer until the sauce is reduced by about half. Taste for salt.
Serve with rice. It is good warm or at room temperature.

tips: Tulingan has a strong taste. Rinsing away the blood and simmering it long and slowly makes it milder.

title: Sinaing na tulingan
intro: Bullet tuna packed into a pot with dried kamias, salt and pork fat and simmered for hours until the bones soften and the liquid is absorbed. The fish turns dense, salty and sour, and a little goes a long way with rice.

steps.text: Rinse the fish well, washing away the blood along the backbone. Rub each one inside and out with some of the salt.
Line the bottom and sides of a heavy pot or clay palayok with the banana leaves, then lay half the pork fat on the bottom.
Pack the fish in tightly, standing or in layers, scattering the kamias and the rest of the salt between them. Top with the remaining pork fat.
Pour in enough water to just cover the fish. Bring to a boil over medium heat.
Cover, turn the heat to the lowest setting and simmer without stirring. Add a little hot water only if the pot is drying out before the bones are soft.
Uncover and simmer until the liquid has almost completely cooked away. Test a fish: the backbone should crush easily between your fingers.
Let it cool in the pot before lifting the fish out. Serve with rice, or fry pieces in a little oil until crisp.

tips: Sinaing keeps a week in the fridge thanks to the salt and sour kamias. For a version without pork, skip the fat and add 2 tablespoons of cooking oil.

title: Ginisang tinapa
intro: Flaked smoked fish sautéed with garlic, onion and lots of tomatoes until saucy. It is smoky, salty and a little sweet from the tomatoes, a cheap ulam that stretches a few fish across a family meal.

steps.text: Pull the skin off the smoked fish, lift the flesh off the bones and flake it, picking out the fine bones.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and sauté the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the tomatoes and cook, pressing them down, until they break into a chunky sauce.
Stir in the flaked fish and the water. Simmer until the fish has soaked up the sauce.
Season with the pepper, taste before adding any salt, and scatter the scallions on top. Serve with rice.

tips: Smoked fish varies a lot in saltiness, so taste before seasoning. Two beaten eggs stirred in at the end make it go further.

title: Tinapa flakes
intro: Smoked fish flaked and slowly toasted in garlic oil until dry and crisp. Spoon it over rice, mix it into fried rice or eat it with tomatoes; a jar lasts for many meals.

steps.text: Skin the fish, lift the flesh off the bones and flake it finely with your fingers, picking out every bone you can feel.
Put the oil and garlic in a cold wide pan and set it over medium-low heat. Stir until the garlic is pale gold.
Add the flaked fish and stir constantly, breaking up clumps, until the flakes are dry, golden and crisp.
Stir in the chili flakes, sugar and pepper and cook for another minute.
Spread on a tray to cool completely, then pack into a clean, dry jar.

tips: Keep the heat low and keep stirring: the flakes go from golden to burnt quickly at the end. Stored airtight, they last 2 weeks in the fridge.

title: Tortang tinapa
intro: Smoked fish flakes folded into beaten eggs with tomato and onion, then fried into small golden omelets. The smoke comes through every bite, and banana ketchup is the usual dip.

steps.text: Beat the eggs in a bowl. Stir in the fish flakes, onion, tomato, scallions and pepper. The fish is salty, so hold off on salt.
Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a nonstick pan over medium heat.
Ladle in about 0.333 cup of the mixture per omelet, spreading the fish evenly. Fry until the edges set and the underside is golden.
Turn and fry the other side until set. Repeat with the rest, adding oil as needed.
Serve hot with rice and banana ketchup.

tips: Leftover ginisang tinapa or tinapa flakes work just as well as fresh flakes here.

title: Ginisang tuyo with tomatoes
intro: Crisp fried dried herring tossed with garlic, onion and juicy tomatoes cooked down with a splash of vinegar. The tomatoes soften the saltiness, making it a filling ulam from a few pantry staples.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and fry the tuyo until crisp, a few at a time. Drain and break each into 2 or 3 pieces.
Pour off all but 2 tablespoons of oil. Sauté the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the tomatoes and cook until soft and juicy.
Add the vinegar and let it bubble without stirring, then season with the pepper and the sugar if the tomatoes are sharp.
Return the tuyo and toss until coated. Serve right away with rice, while the fish still has some crunch.

tips: Fry tuyo with the kitchen window open; the smell is strong. Do not add salt.

title: Gourmet tuyo
intro: Boneless dried herring fillets kept in garlicky olive oil with chilies, peppercorns and bay leaves. Tuyo in oil is salty and spicy, eaten straight from the jar with rice or tossed with pasta.

items.name: olive oil
items.note: or half olive oil, half corn oil

steps.text: Soak the tuyo in warm water to soften slightly and remove some salt, then drain and pat dry.
Pull off the heads, peel away the skin and lift the fillets off the bones in pieces.
Heat 3 tablespoons of the oil in a pan over medium heat and fry the fillets until lightly golden. Lift them out.
Add the rest of the oil, the garlic, chilies, peppercorns and bay leaves to the pan. Warm over low heat until the garlic is soft and just starting to color.
Return the fillets and keep on low heat so the flavors meld, without letting the oil bubble hard.
Cool completely, then pack the fish into clean, dry jars and pour the oil and aromatics over to cover.

tips: Use a clean, dry spoon every time and keep the fish under the oil. Refrigerated, it keeps about a month.

title: Pritong danggit
intro: Split dried rabbitfish fried for seconds until golden and crackling. It is salty, slightly sweet and very crisp, made for rice, spiced vinegar and sliced tomatoes.

steps.text: Separate any danggit stuck together and trim off ragged fins with scissors.
Mix the vinegar, garlic and chilies for the dip.
Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Fry the danggit a few at a time, pressing them flat, until golden. It only takes seconds per side.
Drain on paper towels, where they crisp further as they cool slightly.
Serve with the spiced vinegar, tomatoes and rice.

tips: Danggit burns quickly because it is thin and a little sweet. Keep the heat at medium and pull it the moment it turns golden.

title: Crispy dilis
intro: Dried anchovies fried until golden and crunchy, served with a tomato and onion salad and spiced vinegar. It is salty and crunchy, and a small plate goes a long way with rice.

steps.text: Put the dilis in a sieve and shake off loose salt and broken bits. Pick out any debris.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat. Add a test anchovy: it should sizzle gently, not violently.
Fry the dilis in two batches, stirring, until golden and crisp. Lift out with a slotted spoon onto paper towels.
Toss the tomatoes and onion together and mix the vinegar with the garlic.
Serve the dilis with the tomato salad, the vinegar and rice.

tips: Dilis darkens a shade more after it leaves the oil, so take it out when light golden.

title: Sweet and spicy dilis
intro: Crisp fried anchovies tossed in a sticky glaze of caramelized sugar, garlic and chili. Each bite is sweet, salty and hot, good with rice or as pulutan.

steps.text: Shake the dilis in a sieve to remove loose salt. Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and fry the dilis in batches until crisp and golden. Drain.
Pour off all but 2 tablespoons of oil. Over low heat, cook the garlic until pale gold.
Add the sugar, chili flakes and water and stir until the sugar melts and bubbles into a syrup.
Turn off the heat, add the dilis and toss quickly until every piece is coated.
Spread on a tray lined with parchment to cool and harden, then break up any clumps. Store airtight.

tips: Work fast once the dilis go into the syrup; it sets as it cools. Stored airtight, it stays crisp for a week.

title: Tortang dulong
intro: Tiny silverfish bound with egg and a little flour and fried into lacy, golden fritters. They are soft inside, crisp at the edges and good with vinegar or banana ketchup.

steps.text: Press the drained dulong gently in a sieve to remove as much water as possible.
Mix the eggs, flour, onion, scallions, salt and pepper into a smooth batter, then fold in the dulong.
Heat a few tablespoons of the oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Drop in heaped spoonfuls of the mixture and flatten slightly.
Fry until the edges are golden and crisp, then turn and fry the other side. Drain and repeat, adding oil as needed.
Serve hot with spiced vinegar or banana ketchup and rice.

tips: Dulong is sold fresh or frozen in packs. Thaw frozen dulong in the fridge and drain it very well, or the fritters will spatter and fall apart.

title: Fish cakes
intro: Patties of minced white fish with carrot, onion and scallions, pan-fried until golden and springy. They are mild and lightly sweet, served with a vinegar dip or sweet chili sauce.

steps.text: Cut the fish into chunks and pulse in a food processor into a sticky paste, or mince it very finely with a knife.
Add the egg, cornstarch, flour, salt, sugar and pepper and mix hard with a spoon for a minute, until the paste turns springy.
Fold in the onion, garlic, carrot and scallions. Fry a small spoonful to taste for seasoning.
With oiled hands, shape the mixture into 12 patties about 1 cm thick.
Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat and fry the patties in batches until golden on both sides and puffed.
Drain and serve with spiced vinegar or sweet chili sauce and rice.

tips: Mixing the paste hard before adding the vegetables gives the cakes their bouncy bite. Chill the mixture for 15 minutes if it is too soft to shape.

title: Tuna patties
intro: Canned tuna mashed with potato, carrot and onion, shaped into patties, crumbed and fried until crisp. They are soft and savory inside, a cheap ulam that children like with ketchup.

items.name: eggs
items.note: 1 in the mix, 1 beaten for coating

steps.text: Mix the tuna, mashed potatoes, onion, carrot, 1 egg, salt and pepper until evenly combined.
Shape into 8 patties about 1.5 cm thick. Chill them so they hold their shape.
Dip each patty in the beaten egg, then coat in breadcrumbs.
Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Fry the patties in batches until golden and crisp, turning once.
Drain on paper towels and serve with banana ketchup and rice.

tips: Mash the potatoes while hot and let them cool before mixing; warm potato makes a sticky mix.

title: Ginisang sardinas with egg
intro: Canned sardines in tomato sauce sautéed with garlic, onion and fresh tomato, then folded with soft scrambled egg. It is a quick, saucy ulam made from pantry staples.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat. Sauté the garlic and onion until soft, then add the tomato and cook until it softens.
Add the sardines with their sauce and the water. Break the fish into large chunks with the spoon and simmer.
Pour the eggs over the sardines. Let them set for a moment, then fold gently so they cook into soft curds.
Season with the pepper, scatter the scallions on top and serve with rice.

tips: Canned sardines are already salty. Taste before adding any fish sauce or salt.

title: Sardinas with eggplant
intro: Soft eggplant simmered with canned sardines in tomato sauce, garlic and onion. The eggplant absorbs the savory sauce, making a filling ulam on a budget.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Sauté the garlic and onion until soft, then add the tomato and cook until it collapses.
Add the eggplant and stir to coat in the oil. Cook until it starts to soften.
Add the sardines with their sauce and the water. Break the fish into chunks, cover and simmer until the eggplant is tender.
Season with fish sauce and pepper to taste and serve with rice.

tips: Stir gently once the eggplant is soft so it does not turn to mush. Two beaten eggs folded in at the end are a common addition.

title: Ampalaya with sardinas
intro: Thinly sliced bitter gourd sautéed with canned sardines, tomato and egg. The sardine sauce and egg soften the bitterness, so even ampalaya doubters often like this one.

steps.text: Toss the sliced bitter gourd with the salt and let it sit.
Squeeze the bitter gourd firmly by the handful to press out the juice, rinse once and squeeze again.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat. Sauté the garlic, onion and tomato until soft.
Add the bitter gourd and stir-fry until bright green and just tender.
Add the sardines with their sauce, break them up and simmer briefly.
Pour in the eggs, let them set slightly, then fold gently. Season with pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Do not stir the bitter gourd too much while it cooks; it releases more bitterness when overworked.

title: Upo with sardinas
intro: Tender strips of bottle gourd simmered with canned sardines, garlic and tomatoes into a light, mildly sweet ulam with plenty of sauce to pour over rice.

items.name: medium upo (bottle gourd)
items.note: about 800 g, peeled, seeded and cut into strips

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat. Sauté the garlic, onion and tomatoes until the tomatoes are soft.
Add the sardines with their sauce and break them into chunks.
Add the upo and the water, stir, cover and simmer until the upo turns translucent and tender.
Season with fish sauce and pepper and serve hot with rice.

tips: Upo gives off a lot of water as it cooks, so start with little liquid. A handful of misua stirred in at the end makes it more filling.

title: Pechay with sardinas
intro: Pechay stems and leaves sautéed quickly with canned sardines, garlic and onion. The greens stay crisp and juicy in the savory tomato sauce, and it is ready in about twenty minutes.

items.name: bunches pechay (bok choy)
items.note: about 500 g, stems and leaves separated, cut into 5 cm pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Sauté the garlic, onion and tomato until soft.
Add the sardines with their sauce and the water and break the fish into chunks. Bring to a simmer.
Add the pechay stems first and cook until just tender.
Add the leaves and toss until wilted but still bright green. Season with pepper, taste for salt and serve with rice.

tips: Pechay overcooks quickly. Take the pan off the heat as soon as the leaves wilt.

title: Sardinas with misua
intro: Canned sardines simmered with garlic, onion and patola, then thickened with thin misua noodles. It is a soupy, comforting ulam ladled over rice, especially on rainy days.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat and sauté the garlic until golden, then the onion until soft.
Add the sardines with their sauce and the water. Break the fish into chunks and bring to a boil.
Add the patola and simmer until tender.
Break the misua into the pot and stir gently until soft and the soup thickens slightly.
Season with fish sauce and pepper, scatter the scallions on top and serve right away with rice.

tips: Misua keeps absorbing liquid as it sits. Cook it just before eating, and add a splash of hot water when reheating.

title: Tortang tuna
intro: Canned tuna mixed into beaten eggs with onion and tomato and fried into small, fluffy omelets. It is quick and savory, and banana ketchup is the classic dip.

steps.text: Beat the eggs with the flour until smooth. Stir in the tuna, onion, tomato, salt and pepper.
Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a nonstick pan over medium heat.
Ladle in about 0.333 cup of the mixture per omelet and spread it into a round. Fry until the edges set and the underside is golden.
Turn and fry the other side. Repeat with the rest, adding oil as needed.
Serve hot with rice and banana ketchup.

tips: Press the tuna dry in a sieve before mixing; excess oil makes the omelets greasy and hard to turn.

title: Tuna afritada
intro: Canned tuna chunks simmered in tomato sauce with potatoes, carrots, bell pepper and peas, cooked the way afritada usually is. It is hearty, mildly sweet and made almost entirely from the pantry.

items.name: cans tuna chunks in water or oil

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat. Sauté the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the potatoes and carrot and stir for a couple of minutes so they pick up the flavor.
Add the tomato sauce, water, bay leaf, fish sauce and sugar. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer until the potatoes are just tender.
Add the tuna, bell pepper and peas. Simmer gently, without breaking up the tuna too much, until the sauce thickens.
Taste for salt and sugar, remove the bay leaf and serve with rice.

tips: Add the tuna last: it is already cooked and only needs to heat through, so long simmering turns it to shreds.
